comments.author: mistersquid
comments.story_title: Winners Take All: The Elite Charade of Changing the World [video]
comments.why_zh: 这场爆炸性的演讲挑战 Google 公开其政治活动
comments.quote_zh: 视频前半段的质量非常出色。
comments.text_zh: Giridharadas 的演讲在思想观点上极具爆炸性。据我所知，尽管他是受邀到 Google 园区（波士顿）演讲的，但他一点也没留情面。在 29:03 处，Giridharadas 向听众发出挑战，要求他们敦促 Google（以及其他硅谷公司）每年向员工——也就是他台下这些听众——公开政治披露信息。[0] 顺便说一句，Giridharadas 的表达非常清晰、有分寸，我发现把视频调到 1.5 倍速是个很舒服的观看速度（个人体验，仅供参考）。在我提到的时间点之前，Giridharadas 讲的内容同样具有挑衅性，在政治上是冒险的。我还没法评论他的整场演讲，但视频前半段的质量非常出色。[0] [视频]
comments.text: Giridharadas talk is explosive in terms of its ideas. From what I can tell, he's not pulling any punches even though he's been invited to speak on a Google campus (Boston). At 29:03 Giridharadas challenges his audience to demand that Google (and other Silicon Valley companies) generate an annual political disclosure to its employees, the very people in his audience. [0] As a side note, Giridharadas is very clear and measured in his articulation, and I found that speeding the video to 1.5 times normal rate to be a good delivery speed (YMMV). What Giridharadas says prior to the timecode I referenced is also provocative and politically risky. I can't yet comment on his entire talk, but the quality of the first half the video is superb. [0] [VIDEO]

comments.story_title: Adding Up the Cost of Tax Breaks for Big Tech’s Data Centers (2016)
comments.why_zh: 说明“双赢”框架如何把讨论的范围收窄
comments.quote_zh: Anand Giridharadas 最近做了一场很棒的演讲[1]（就在 Google！）
comments.text_zh: > “双赢”（公司拿到补贴，地区得到就业）Anand Giridharadas 最近做了一场很棒的演讲[1]（就在 Google！），他在其中解释了“双赢”如何是一种障眼法，用来设定对话的框架。把一个方案（比如补贴）框定为对所有人都有好处，在观感上很讨喜，但它暗含地制造了一种只考虑该方案的框架。（要么是这个方案，要么“你什么也得不到”。）如果不加这种受限的框架，选择并不是二元的“补贴或什么都没有”；这笔钱有很多种花法。（例如，也许不要那家企业，转而投资教育或基础设施，会带来更大的好处。）[1] [视频]
comments.text: > “win win” (company gets subsidy, area gets jobs) Anand Giridharadas recently gave an a great talk[1] (at Google!) in which he explains how "win win" is a charade used to set the framing of the conversation. Framing a plan (like a subsidy) as something that benefits everyone has good optics, but it implicitly creates a framing that only considers that plan. (it's either this plan or "you get nothing"). Without the restricted framing, the choice isn't a binary "subsidies or nothing"; there are many ways that money could be spent. (e.g. maybe going without that business and investing in education or infrastructure would provide a greater benefit). [1] [VIDEO]

comments.text: I read this book and, to be honest, did not enjoy it very much. It consists largely of profiles of people involved in this sort of philanthrocapitalism. The main theme seems to be that the ultra-wealthy have coopted the work of social institutions in such a way as to undermine efforts for truly revolutionary change, that is change that might threaten them. The premise is interesting but the content is pretty boring. I got tired of reading about people whom the author believes to be mislead or malicious or otherwise on the wrong path. For those interested he gave a talk at Google in Cambridge that was pretty good. [VIDEO]

comments.text_zh: “这些新慈善家给慈善带来了‘创业型倾向’，Hay 和 Muller 在 2014 年的一篇论文中写道，但他们认为这种倾向‘把注意力和资源从当代资本主义种种表现的缺陷上转移开’，并且还可能替代了国家撤出的公共支出。本质上，我们正在目睹的是公共产品和服务的责任从民主机构转移到富人手中，再由一个高管阶层来管理。在 CEO 社会里，履行社会责任这件事的讨论，不再围绕企业是否应该承担超出自身商业利益的责任。相反，讨论的是如何利用慈善来强化一个政治经济体系，而这个体系让如此少数的人得以积累天文数字的财富。扎克伯格投资解决湾区住房危机，就是这一大趋势的一个例子。”[1] 不过，从你说的“详尽到令人痛苦的程度”来看，你似乎之前已经看过这些证据，却不知为何不愿承认这个制度的缺陷。最后这部分只是观察，并非负面的价值判断。这段 Anand Giridharadas 的视频也很棒：[VIDEO]，还有他的书《Winners Take All: The Elite Charade of Changing the World》。[1] [LINK]
comments.text: "These new philanthropists bring to charity an “entrepreneurial disposition”, Hay and Muller wrote in a 2014 paper, yet one that they suggest has been “diverting attention and resources away from the failings of contemporary manifestations of capitalism”, and may also be serving as a substitute for public spending withdrawn by the state. Essentially, what we are witnessing is the transfer of responsibility for public goods and services from democratic institutions to the wealthy, to be administered by an executive class. In the CEO society, the exercise of social responsibilities is no longer debated in terms of whether corporations should or shouldn’t be responsible for more than their own business interests. Instead, it is about how philanthropy can be used to reinforce a politico-economic system that enables such a small number of people to accumulate obscene amounts of wealth. Zuckerberg’s investment in solutions to the Bay Area housing crisis is an example of this broader trend." [1] Although with your "in excruciating detail" it sounds like you've been presented with the evidence before, yet you are somehow unwilling to admit the failings of the system. This last part is meant as an observation and not as a negative value judgement. This video with Anand Giridharadas is also great: [VIDEO] , as well as his book 'Winners Take All: The Elite Charade of Changing the World'. [1] [LINK]

comments.author: brigandish
comments.story_title: The YouTube ban is un-American, wrong, and will backfire
comments.why_zh: 被引用来支持关于赢家的慈善保护体系的观点
comments.text_zh: > 最后，还有“审查”这个词。这是一个带指责意味的词，被那些以为自己拥有某种并不存在的“言论自由”的人使用。第一修正案适用于美国政府与其公民之间的约定，并不适用于你与 YouTube 的关系。 > YouTube 是一家公司，它与用户之间有完全独立的约定，其中并不包含言论自由。因此，按定义来说，这并不是审查。第一修正案和言论自由并不是同义词，很明显，因为在美国政府管辖范围之外也可以存在言论自由；同样，YouTube 是一家跨国企业，使用它的也不只是美国公民。即使它完全处于美国管辖之内、且只服务美国公民，第一修正案仍然不是言论自由的同义词。censor 一词源自拉丁语中古罗马的一个政府职位，但这并不意味着因此所有审查都只能或只能由政府实施。这不仅在逻辑上没有支撑，在实践中也不成立。像 Twitter[1]、Facebook[2] 和 Google[3] 这样的公司，会出于政治上的便利（或者，正如 Anand Giridharadas 所指出的[4]，出于任何便利）从它们的平台上移除内容： > 当你审视我们这个时代的赢家如何回馈、如何帮忙、如何带来改变时，你会发现这些做法往往是为了保护这个体系——尤其是——赢家们所立足其上的那个体系。
comments.text: > And finally, the word “censorship”. This is an accusatory word used by people who think it relates to their non-existent “freedom of speech”. The first amendment applies to the agreement between the US government and its citizens. It does not apply to your relationship with YouTube. > YouTube is a corporation that has an entirely separate agreement with its users, which does not include freedom of speech. Therefore, it’s not censorship — by definition. The first amendment and freedom of speech are not synonyms, quite obviously because there can be freedom of speech outside of the jurisdiction of the US government; and similarly, Youtube is a trans-national corporation with more than just US citizens using it. Even if it were wholly within US jurisdiction and Youtube only served US citizens, the first amendment is still not a synonym for freedom of speech. The word censor comes from a Latin word for a governmental position in ancient Rome but it does not follow that all censorship is therefore only possible or enacted by government. Not only is there no supporting logic for that, it's not evident in practice . Companies like Twitter[1], Facebook[2] and Google[3] remove things from their platforms for political convenience (or, as Anand Giridharadas points out[4], for any convenience): > When you look at the ways in which the winners of our age give back, help out, make a difference, they are often designed to protect the system - above all - that the winners stand on top of.
